newsitem.title: FRANCE: Five-day lecture to replace French conscription.
newsitem.headline: Five-day lecture to replace French conscription.

text.p: The French government on Wednesday approved a plan to replace military service with a mere five days of civic lectures when it abolishes conscription in 2002.

A bill passed by the cabinet said all young people would be subject to a census at age 16 and would be summoned to a five-day "rendezvous citoyen" (civic meeting) -- a course on Republican institutions and defence -- between 18 and 25.

"Conscription, which once was fully justified, no longer meets military needs nor the characteristics of modern society," President Jacques Chirac told the centre-right cabinet, according to government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.
Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen blasted the civic meeting as intended to conceal a dismantling of France's armed forces after the Cold War.
The move towards all-professional armed forces, part of a deep defence reform designed to modernise the military and increase its capacity for long-term actions overseas, was announced last year.
The government had yet to unveil specific plans for what it would substitute for the military service. The plans will go before parliament.

Conscription, dating back to 1793, involves more than 400,000 men every year. Its duration had gradually been cut to under a year as it became increasingly unpopular among many young men who felt they were wasting time which should be spent looking for jobs.

France's overall military strength will drop from half a million to 350,000 when the move to all-professional forces is completed in 2002, with the number of troops serving abroad being cut to 39,000 from 56,000.
The streamlining of the armed forces will mean disbanding 38 regiments, many in Germany, closing barracks, army hospitals and air bases and retiring one of two aircraft carriers.
Civic meetings will start as experiments from next year for young men and from 2003 for young women.
The gatherings will also allow authorities to keep tabs on the young people's background and education for statistics.

Volunteers aged 18 to 30 will enlist for a nine-months to two-year national service either in the armed forces, or as civilian social workers in France and overseas territories, or abroad in humanitarian and development work.

Chirac said a volunteer national service would remain and could provide a second chance for young people who failed to get a good start in adult life. He said as many young people as possible would serve abroad to give them wider experience.
